title: Reduce contention in continuous-batch controller and cache coordinator
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Problem:

Our continuous-batching controller and the cache coordination layer are a frequent source of CPU contention and tail latency variance when model concurrency spikes. Symptoms observed in production and in recent canaries: periodic 95/99th token latency spikes under blended workloads, frequent scheduler stalls when many small requests arrive simultaneously, and steady increase in mutex hold times in the cache coordinator thread.

Background: the current implementation centralizes batch queue state and cache invalidation in a single controller guarded by a coarse global lock. Continuous batching relies on a monolithic state machine that tries to serve multiple models and sequence lengths. This design simplifies correctness but amplifies contention as we scale Dedicated pools and run multi-tenant workloads.

Goals:
- Remove the global lock hotspot and replace with per-model, sharded controllers for continuous batching.
- Extract cache coordination into a lock-free (or low-lock) coordinator using epoch-based invalidation and read-optimized paths for KV reads.
- Reduce scheduler hold times and improve headroom for sudden concurrency spikes without changing external API semantics.
- Keep regressions under 5% for average latency while improving p99 token latency by at least 15% on representative blends.

Proposed approach:
1) Controller sharding: introduce a per-model batch controller keyed by (model_id, batch_lane) with an efficient fast-path for single-request arrivals. Controllers communicate via non-blocking ring buffers for cross-controller fallback rather than a global queue.
2) Cache coordinator rewrite: implement an epoch-based cache invalidation strategy. Readers use an atomic epoch check + pointer to current shard, writers bump epoch and install a new shard reference. For small writes we batch invalidations into micro-epochs to avoid frequent barriers.
3) Scheduler cleanup: separate admission control from commit path. Admission decisions will be made with best-effort heuristics and lightweight token buckets; commit path is where persistence to metrics and tracing happens asynchronously.
4) Dependency upgrades: upgrade tokio to 1.25 for improved task parking and timers; upgrade crossbeam to latest stable to use SegQueue improvements; bump jemalloc shim for more predictable allocation in high-concurrency tails. Track these upgrades in a separate PR and test for regressions in alloc profiles.
5) Observability and safety: add fine-grained metrics (lock hold time histograms, epoch churn counter, per-controller queue depth) and a feature flag that gates the new controller per pool so we can canary rollout.

Non-goals:
- Changing model scheduling policy or preemption semantics.
- Large-scale redesign of autoscaling logic (only minor hooks for controller-driven hints).

Acceptance criteria:
- Unit + stress tests proving correctness for epoch invalidation and no stale reads (CI must pass without flakiness for 72-hour stress runs).
- Benchmarks on the perf cluster showing >=15% improvement in p99 token latency and <=5% regression on average latency for the standard blended workload (blend-v2).
- No increase in OOM incidents on Dedicated canaries; allocation profile within 10% of baseline.
- Canary rollout plan executed: 5% traffic -> 20% -> 50% -> 100% with rollback automated on SLO breach.

Migration/rollout plan:
- Step 0: Merge refactor behind feature flag; run extended CI stress tests and perf microbenchmarks.
- Step 1: Canary on internal staging pools with synthetic blended traffic for 48h.
- Step 2: Canary to 5% production traffic in non-critical regions for 24h with watchlist alerts for lock hold time and p99.
- Step 3: Expand to 20% and wait 72h; verify billing/cost signals to ensure no hidden cost increase from sharding artifacts.
- Step 4: Full rollout if metrics stable.

Rollback triggers:
- p99 token latency increases >10% over baseline for three consecutive one-hour windows.
- Error rate increase >0.5% absolute or any new 5xx pattern emerging.
- Memory/alloc pressure surpasses Canary limits.

Notes on testing and artifacts:
- Perf harness: https://perf.redwood.internal/dashboards/continuous-batch-refactor (read-only for engineers)
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/ENG/Per-model+batcher+and+epoch+cache+coordination
- PRs: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving/pull/3621 (controller sharding) and https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving/pull/3629 (epoch-based cache coordinator).

Longer term follow-ups (post-merge):
- Explore per-tenant cache size heuristics and adaptive micro-epoch lengths based on write churn.
- Consider tying controller sharding to capacity-aware placement to further reduce cross-host fallbacks.
- Evaluate replacing jemalloc shim with a tuned system allocator on certain Dedicated SKUs if allocation tail persists.
